channel.title: Research on Best of AI
channel.description: Recent content in Research on Best of AI

item.title: arXiv
item.description:
Authors upload papers, and readers can search, download, and set up alerts. Cornell University operates it. Most papers in physics and math appear there first.

Papers are not peer reviewed by arXiv itself, so quality varies.

bioRxiv and SSRN serve other fields. arXiv suits physicists and mathematicians.

item.title: ATLAS.ti
item.description:
It supports document coding, memos, networks, and co-occurrence tables. AI coding and summary features suggest codes and condense text, and researchers can accept or edit them. It runs on desktop and in a browser.

It is used in academic research, UX research, and market research. Licenses are sold in student, academic, and business tiers.

NVivo and MAXQDA are the main alternatives. ATLAS.ti suits researchers who want flexible coding and visual network tools.

item.title: BioRender
item.description:
Researchers drag icons into a canvas and edit them to build pathways, experimental workflows, and graphical abstracts. Templates speed up common layouts, and teams share a library. Paid plans allow publication use and export options.

Free accounts have limits on exports and icons, so check the license before publishing.

Illustrator and Inkscape give more freedom but take more time. BioRender suits biologists and biochemists.

item.title: CAS SciFinder
item.description:
Users search by structure, reaction, or keyword and see papers, patents, and suppliers. Retrosynthesis tools suggest routes to a target molecule. Results link to the CAS registry.

Access is by subscription, usually through institutions.

Reaxys is the main alternative. SciFinder suits chemists doing literature and synthesis research.

item.title: ChemDraw
item.description:
Users draw structures, predict properties like NMR shifts, and name compounds from drawings. It integrates with Revvity Signals tools and Microsoft Office. A web version supports sharing.

Licenses are paid, and many universities provide them.

MarvinSketch and Ketcher are alternatives. ChemDraw suits synthetic and medicinal chemists.

item.title: Covidence
item.description:
Two reviewers screen independently, and conflicts are resolved in the tool. It supports risk-of-bias assessment and data extraction forms. It records PRISMA-style counts as the review proceeds.

It is subscription-based, and many universities hold licenses.

Rayyan is an alternative. Covidence suits clinical researchers running systematic reviews.

item.title: Findmypast
item.description:
Users search census, parish, and military records, and view images of the original documents. Family trees are shared and linked to records. Hints suggest matches.

It is a subscription service.

Ancestry and MyHeritage are alternatives. Findmypast suits genealogists with British and Irish ancestry.

item.title: GraphPad Prism
item.description:
Users enter data in tables, choose analyses such as t-tests, ANOVA, survival curves, or nonlinear regression, and get publication-style graphs. It guides non-statisticians with explanations of results. Dose-response and kinetics fitting are common uses.

It is a paid license, often provided through universities. It is less flexible than R or Python for custom work.

R, Python, and JMP are alternatives. Prism suits bench scientists who want a quick path from data to figure.

item.title: MATLAB
item.description:
It has built-in tools for matrices, signal processing, control design, and statistics. Toolboxes add machine learning, computer vision, and domain-specific functions. MATLAB can generate C code for embedded targets, and an AI assistant helps write code in newer releases.

It is standard in aerospace, automotive, and academic engineering. Licenses cost money, though many universities provide them to students, and Octave and Python are free alternatives.

MATLAB suits engineers who need validated toolboxes and a well-documented workflow.

item.title: NASA ADS
item.description:
Researchers search by author, object, or topic, and export references to BibTeX and other formats. It shows citations and metrics, and links to the full text where available. Libraries and observatories also use its API.

It is run by the Smithsonian Astrophysical Observatory with NASA support. Coverage outside its core fields is thinner.

Semantic Scholar and Google Scholar are broader. NASA ADS suits astronomers and astrophysicists.

item.title: Naviance
item.description:
Students explore colleges, build lists, and request transcripts and recommendations. Counselors track deadlines and see how past applicants from the school fared. Career assessments help students explore paths.

Schools and districts buy access, so individuals cannot usually sign up on their own.

Scoir is a close alternative. Naviance suits school-based admissions counselors.

item.title: NVivo
item.description:
Researchers import text, audio, video, and PDFs, then tag passages with codes and look for themes. Queries, matrices, and visual maps help compare groups and cases. Newer versions include AI-assisted coding and summaries, which researchers should still check.

Social scientists, health researchers, and market researchers use it for projects with many sources. It is expensive for individuals, though universities often hold site licenses.

ATLAS.ti and MAXQDA are close alternatives. NVivo suits researchers who need an organized system for large qualitative projects.

item.title: PhilPapers
item.description:
Users browse by category, search for papers, and set up alerts. Many entries link to open access copies. Categories are curated by volunteer editors.

It is free and community run.

Google Scholar and the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy cover related ground. PhilPapers suits philosophers.

item.title: Praat
item.description:
Users load recordings, view spectrograms, annotate segments, and run scripts for batch analysis. It also supports speech synthesis experiments. The interface is old-fashioned but very capable.

It is open source and runs on Windows, macOS, and Linux.

ELAN is useful for annotating video and audio. Praat suits linguists studying phonetics.

item.title: Publishers Marketplace
item.description:
Literary agents use it to see which editors buy which kinds of books and to post their own deals. Authors use it to research agents. A daily newsletter lists new book deals.

Data is mostly reported by members, so it is not a complete record.

Query Tracker helps authors track submissions. Publishers Marketplace suits literary agents.

item.title: Scoir
item.description:
Counselors manage student lists and send transcripts to colleges electronically. Students compare schools and track deadlines. Colleges share information directly with students who show interest.

Schools adopt it, and the student side is free.

Naviance is the main alternative. Scoir suits college admissions counselors.

item.title: Sketch Engine
item.description:
Users search for words and phrases, see collocations, and compare usage across corpora. A word sketch summarizes grammatical patterns for a word. Users can also build corpora from their own texts.

It is a subscription service, with free access for some academic users.

AntConc is a free desktop alternative. Sketch Engine suits linguists and terminologists.

item.title: Stellarium
item.description:
Users pick a location and date to see stars, planets, and satellites, and can control telescopes through plug-ins. It includes sky cultures and deep sky catalogs.

A web version runs in the browser, and desktop apps exist for Windows, macOS, and Linux.

Cartes du Ciel is another open-source option. Stellarium suits astronomers and amateur observers.

item.title: Wolfram Mathematica
item.description:
Users work in notebooks that combine code, results, and text. The Wolfram Language has built-in functions for a huge range of math and data tasks. It connects with Wolfram Alpha knowledge and, in newer versions, with language model tools.

Licenses are paid, and student editions are cheaper.

MATLAB and SageMath are alternatives. Mathematica suits mathematicians who need symbolic power.

item.title: WorldCat
item.description:
Users search for books, articles, and media, then see which nearby libraries own a copy. Librarians use the underlying records for cataloging and interlibrary loan. OCLC runs the service for member libraries.

Records vary in quality between contributing libraries.

Library of Congress and Google Books are other sources. WorldCat suits librarians and researchers hunting for physical items.

item.title: FamilySearch
item.description:
FamilySearch lets anyone explore their family history without paying. Users search a vast collection of historical records, including census, birth, marriage, death, immigration, and military records, from many countries, and many are digitized images. A collaborative family tree combines contributions from millions of people, so you can often find relatives and connect with branches others have researched.

Technology plays a large role in making records searchable. Handwriting recognition and machine learning transcribe and index scanned documents at scale, which has opened up collections that would take volunteers years to index by hand. Tools suggest possible record matches for people in your tree, and photo and story features preserve family memories. The service also operates local centers and online help.

item.title: FutureHouse
item.description:
FutureHouse works on automating scientific research. The lab builds language-model agents that read and reason over the research literature, and makes some available to scientists on a platform. Crow answers questions with cited sources from papers, Falcon performs deeper literature reviews, and Owl helps check whether a topic has been studied.

A more ambitious project, Robin, links agents into a multi-step workflow. Agents suggest hypotheses, plan experiments, and analyze results, and the lab used the system to propose a candidate treatment, which was then tested experimentally. The goal is to speed up discovery by letting agents handle parts of the loop.

item.title: Maltego
item.description:
Maltego is known for visual link analysis. An investigator starts with an entity such as a domain name, email address, or company, then runs transforms that pull related data from sources like DNS records, social media, breach databases, and corporate registries. The results appear as a graph that shows how things connect, which makes patterns easier to see than in a list.

The tool is widely used in cybersecurity and open-source intelligence work. Threat analysts trace infrastructure behind attacks, fraud teams look for networks of related accounts, and journalists and researchers map ownership and connections. A marketplace of data integrations extends what the graph can query, and collaboration features let teams share findings.

item.title: Mendeley
item.description:
Mendeley helps researchers organize the papers they read. Users import PDFs, and the software extracts details such as the title and authors, stores them in a library, and lets them highlight and annotate. A Word plugin inserts citations and builds a reference list in thousands of styles, which saves hours when writing papers and theses.

It has social and discovery elements, including groups for sharing libraries and a catalog of research papers. Syncing across the desktop, web, and mobile keeps a library available wherever you work. Elsevier acquired the company, which led some researchers to prefer open alternatives because of concerns about data and lock-in.

item.title: Scopus
item.description:
Scopus indexes scholarly journals, books, and conference papers across science, technology, medicine, social sciences, and the arts and humanities, and tracks citations among them. Researchers use it to search literature, follow citation trails, and find related work. It’s curated: content must meet quality criteria to be included, which gives the database a reputation for reliability.

Institutions rely on Scopus for research evaluation. It provides author profiles with h-index and other metrics, journal rankings such as CiteScore, and tools for analyzing the output of departments and universities. Funders and universities use these numbers in assessments, rankings, and hiring, which makes the database influential, and sometimes controversial because of the weight put on metrics.

item.title: Web of Science
item.description:
Web of Science is one of the oldest and most influential indexes of scholarly literature. It covers curated sets of journals, conference proceedings, and books and records which works cite which, making it possible to follow ideas forward and backward through the literature. Researchers use it to find relevant papers, track citations, and analyze trends in a field.

Institutions also use its data for research evaluation. Clarivate publishes the Journal Citation Reports, which includes the impact factor, one of the most discussed metrics in academia, and Web of Science supports measures of authors, journals, and institutions. A Research Assistant adds AI-driven features such as natural language search and summaries of results. The selectivity of coverage is a selling point and also a criticism, as it favors certain journals and languages.

item.title: academic-research-skills
item.description:
This repository bundles the following skills:

  • Deep Research: A 13-agent research skill with modes including full, quick, review, and fact-check.
  • Academic Paper: A 12-agent paper-writing skill with modes including plan, outline-only, and revision.
  • Academic Paper Reviewer: A 7-agent multi-perspective review skill with full and re-review modes.
  • Academic Pipeline: A 10-stage orchestrator skill managing the full workflow with integrity verification.

item.title: AstaBrief 8B
item.description: AstaBrief 8B turns a research question and a set of papers into a cited report. Ai2 also added a Fast mode in Asta that uses it.

item.title: GPT-6 Rosalind Research
item.description: OpenAI released GPT-6 Rosalind Research on October 30, 2026, for multistep life sciences research built on GPT-6 reasoning. Access is limited to approved users.

item.title: nature-skills
item.description:
This repository bundles the following skills:

  • nature-reader: Generates a bilingual Chinese-English Markdown reader of a paper with figure-text alignment.
  • nature-polishing: Revises academic text into Nature-style English with consistent terminology.
  • nature-paper2ppt: Converts a research paper into a presentation deck.
  • nature-reviewer: Simulates a blinded, three-reviewer peer review.
  • nature-response: Generates a point-by-point rebuttal to reviewer comments.
  • nature-figure: Produces publication-grade, multi-panel scientific figures.
  • nature-academic-search: Performs multi-source literature search with citation verification.

item.title: RynnUnify
item.description: RynnUnify, from Alibaba’s DAMO Academy, is a 16B embodied multimodal model that pairs an 8B reasoner with an 8B video generator for visual planning.

item.title: scientific-agent-skills
item.description:
This repository bundles the following skills:

  • Bioinformatics & Genomics: 27 skills covering RNA-seq, BioPython, sequence analysis, and population genomics.
  • Cheminformatics: 10 skills covering RDKit, molecular docking, and drug discovery.
  • Clinical Research: 8 skills covering PK/PD modeling and clinical trial analysis.
  • Machine Learning: 14 skills covering PyTorch Lightning, scikit-learn, and time series analysis.
  • Data Analysis & Visualization: 22 skills covering matplotlib, GeoPandas, and network analysis.
  • Scientific Databases: 11 skills providing unified access to 78+ databases including PubChem and UniProt.
  • Laboratory Automation: 6 skills covering Opentrons liquid handling and LIMS integration.
  • Scientific Communication: 27 skills covering literature review, scientific writing, and peer review.

item.title: ClawsGO Science
item.description:
ClawsGO Science goes beyond literature review. The agent can plan an analysis, write and run code in a cloud environment, process datasets, and report results with the steps shown. It is built for scientific work such as data analysis and computational experiments.

Doing the work, not only describing it, can speed up exploratory research. Results still need scrutiny, since an agent can make statistical or coding mistakes, and reproducibility depends on seeing exactly what was run.

item.title: Google Genie
item.description: Genie is a different kind of generative model. Instead of producing a fixed image or video, it creates a world you can explore: describe a scene, and the model generates an environment that responds as you move through it, frame by frame, with the scene staying consistent as you turn around. DeepMind frames world models as a step toward AI that understands how environments behave, with possible uses in games, robotics training, and simulation.

item.title: Ancestry
item.description:
Ancestry is a genealogy service. Users build a family tree and the site suggests matching records, such as birth certificates, census pages, immigration lists, and military files, from its collection. Hints appear as you add relatives, which helps trace lines back through generations.

Technology helps both records and relatives. Handwriting recognition and machine learning transcribe old documents so they become searchable, and the DNA test connects users with genetic relatives and estimates ethnic origins. Members can share trees and message distant cousins, which often breaks through research dead ends.

item.title: Hunchly
item.description:
Hunchly is a browser extension for investigations. As a researcher browses, it saves each page as it appeared, with screenshots, timestamps, and hash values that help show the content has not been altered. Pages are organized into cases, so evidence from a long investigation stays together.

The tool adds notes, tags, and a way to search across captured content. Reports can be generated for sharing or for legal use. It is popular with open-source intelligence investigators, journalists, and fraud and law enforcement analysts who need to preserve content that may disappear.

item.title: MyHeritage
item.description:
MyHeritage is a genealogy service. Users create a tree, and the site suggests matches in historical records and in other members’ trees, helping them find ancestors and living relatives. A DNA test adds ethnicity estimates and connects users with genetic relatives.

The company is known for photo tools. It can colorize black-and-white pictures, enhance old photos, and animate faces in family photographs, which went viral and made genealogy more emotional for many users. Other AI features transcribe and search documents.

item.title: Rayyan
item.description:
Rayyan streamlines a laborious step in evidence synthesis. Researchers import search results from databases, and multiple reviewers screen titles and abstracts, marking papers as included or excluded, often blind to each other’s decisions. The tool tracks conflicts and helps resolve them.

Machine learning ranks the unscreened papers by likelihood of relevance, so the likely includes surface earlier and screening can end sooner. Highlighting of keywords and filtering by terms speeds reading. Newer features use AI to assist with extraction and summaries.

item.title: Reaxys
item.description:
Reaxys is a chemistry research database from Elsevier. A chemist can search by structure, reaction, or property and find experimental data on compounds, along with the reactions used to make them and the sources. This helps plan syntheses and avoid repeating known work.

Predictive synthesis tools propose routes to a target molecule by combining literature data with machine learning, ranking options by feasibility. It also covers properties, bioactivity, and patent chemistry, serving drug discovery and materials work.

item.title: AlphaCode 2
item.description: AlphaCode 2 is Google DeepMind’s competitive-programming system, published as a technical report in December 2023 as a follow-up to the original AlphaCode. Instead of a single model, it is a pipeline built on fine-tuned Gemini models: it samples up to a million candidate C++ solutions per problem, then filters them down through test-based checks, behavioral clustering, and a learned scoring model to pick roughly ten final submissions. On a set of recent Codeforces contests, it solved 43 percent of problems within ten attempts, nearly double the original AlphaCode’s 25 percent.

item.title: AlphaFold 3
item.description: AlphaFold 3 is a structure-prediction model that Google DeepMind and Isomorphic Labs released in May 2024, extending the earlier protein-only AlphaFold 2 to a much wider range of biological molecules. Instead of predicting only protein folds, it jointly models complexes containing proteins, DNA, RNA, small-molecule ligands, ions, and chemically modified residues, using a redesigned architecture built around a module called Pairformer. This lets researchers ask how a candidate drug molecule might bind to a protein, or how a protein interacts with a strand of RNA, in a single prediction rather than stitching together separate tools.

item.title: AlphaGeometry
item.description: AlphaGeometry is a neuro-symbolic system from Google DeepMind, published in Nature in January 2024, built to solve geometry problems at the level of International Mathematical Olympiad competitors. It pairs a language model trained on synthetically generated geometry proofs with a traditional symbolic deduction engine: the neural half proposes useful auxiliary constructions, such as new points or lines, and the symbolic half runs formal logical deduction to complete the proof. On a benchmark of 30 IMO geometry problems from 2000 to 2022, it solved 25, close to the average gold medalist’s score and far ahead of prior automated theorem provers.

item.title: AudioLM
item.description: AudioLM is a research framework that Google published in September 2022, treating audio generation as a language modeling problem over discrete audio tokens instead of the usual spectrogram or waveform regression approaches. It combines two representations: semantic tokens from w2v-BERT, a self-supervised speech model, that capture long-range structure, and acoustic tokens from the SoundStream neural codec that preserve fine audio detail for high-quality synthesis. Trained only on raw audio with no text transcripts or annotations, it can continue a few seconds of spoken audio or piano music in a way that stays coherent over tens of seconds, something earlier audio generation methods struggled with. Google never released it as a product; it stayed a research paper and demo page, and Google DeepMind used its token-based approach as a building block for later work like MusicLM and parts of Lyria.

item.title: BitNet b1.58
item.description: BitNet b1.58 is a line of research from Microsoft exploring language models built from ternary weights, meaning every weight is restricted to -1, 0, or 1 instead of the usual 16- or 32-bit floating point values. The original paper, “The Era of 1-bit LLMs,” came out in February 2024 and showed that models trained natively this way, rather than quantized after the fact, could match full-precision models like Llama 2 at comparable sizes while cutting memory use and inference energy substantially. Microsoft followed up in April 2025 with BitNet b1.58 2B4T, an openly released 2-billion-parameter checkpoint trained on 4 trillion tokens, whose non-embedding memory footprint runs about 0.4GB, well under similarly sized models like Gemma 3 1B or MiniCPM 2B. The weights and inference code are on GitHub and Hugging Face under the MIT license, and the project is notable less for beating other models on benchmarks than for proving that 1-bit training works at all without a big performance penalty, which matters for running capable models on phones or edge devices.

item.title: BlenderBot 3
item.description: BlenderBot 3 is an open-domain chatbot that Meta AI released in August 2022, built on top of Meta’s own OPT-175B language model and fine-tuned to hold conversations, search the web for current information, and remember details across sessions. At 175 billion parameters it was, at the time, the largest publicly released conversational AI model, and Meta made the code, model card, and training data available alongside it, in contrast to closed systems like OpenAI’s models. It was designed to keep improving from real conversations: Meta let members of the public chat with it and collected feedback to retrain and refine it over time, along with safety filters meant to catch toxic or unsafe responses. Full access to the 175B model was restricted to approved researchers, though smaller 3B and 30B versions were released more openly through Meta’s ParlAI framework. It was a research project rather than a commercial product, and its public demo was later shut down; today it’s mostly of historical interest as one of the last major “research chatbot” releases before ChatGPT reset expectations for what a conversational model should do.

item.title: ByT5
item.description: ByT5 is a variant of Google’s T5 text-to-text model that Google Research published in mid-2021, notable for dropping tokenization altogether and operating directly on raw UTF-8 bytes. Standard language models split text into subword tokens using a fixed vocabulary built by a tokenizer, which works well for the languages and scripts that vocabulary was built around but tends to handle rare words, misspellings, and less common languages poorly. ByT5 sidesteps that by treating every input as a sequence of bytes, giving it a vocabulary of only a few hundred possible values instead of tens of thousands of subword tokens.

item.title: Chameleon
item.description: Chameleon is a multimodal model from Meta FAIR, described in a May 2024 paper, that mixes text and images from the ground up rather than bolting a vision encoder onto a language model. Most multimodal systems use “late fusion,” where a separate image encoder feeds visual features into a language model that was pretrained on text alone. Chameleon instead quantizes images into discrete tokens and trains on sequences of interleaved text and image tokens from scratch, so the same transformer learns to reason over both modalities and can also generate images as output, not just describe them.

item.title: Chinchilla
item.description: Chinchilla is a research language model that DeepMind described in a March 2022 paper on compute-optimal training. At 70 billion parameters, it is much smaller than DeepMind’s earlier 280 billion parameter Gopher model, yet Chinchilla was trained on roughly four times more data and beat Gopher, GPT-3, and other larger models of the era on a wide range of benchmarks, including an average MMLU score around 67.5%. The paper’s core finding was that most large language models up to that point were undertrained relative to their size: for a fixed compute budget, model size and training data should scale together, not just model size alone.

item.title: Emu Video
item.description: Emu Video is a text-to-video research model Meta introduced in November 2023, built on top of Meta’s Emu image generator. Rather than generating video directly from a text prompt in one step, it splits the job in two: first it uses Emu to generate a still image from the prompt, then it generates a video conditioned on both the text and that image. Meta reported that this factored approach let it skip the deep cascade of separate models that earlier systems like Google’s Imagen Video and Meta’s own Make-A-Video relied on, while still producing higher-resolution output. In human preference evaluations, Meta said raters favored Emu Video’s clips over Imagen Video’s and Make-A-Video’s the large majority of the time. It was released as a research paper and demo rather than a public product, and its techniques fed into later Meta video features rather than shipping as a standalone model.

item.title: Emu3
item.description: Emu3 is an open-weight multimodal model from the Beijing Academy of Artificial Intelligence, released in September 2024, built around a single idea: treat text, images, and video all as sequences of discrete tokens and train one transformer to predict the next token across all three, with no separate diffusion or CLIP-style component. BAAI released it as an 8B-parameter model in Chat and Gen variants, one tuned for vision-language understanding and one for generation. Despite the simplified single-objective design, BAAI reported that Emu3 outperformed established task-specific open models of the time, including SDXL for image generation and LLaVA-1.6 for vision-language understanding. The project is a predecessor to BAAI’s larger Emu3.5 model, released in late 2025, which scales the same next-token-prediction approach up to 34 billion parameters.

item.title: Flamingo
item.description: Flamingo is a vision-language model DeepMind published in April 2022, built to handle images, videos, and text together and answer open-ended questions about them after seeing only a handful of examples. It starts from Chinchilla, DeepMind’s 70B parameter language model, and adds vision encoders and cross-attention layers that let it condition text generation on visual input, bringing the full model to roughly 80B parameters. The key idea was few-shot learning for vision-language tasks: rather than fine-tuning on each new dataset, Flamingo could be shown a small number of examples in its prompt and generalize from there, similar to how GPT-3 did for text. At release it beat every prior few-shot approach on 16 vision-language benchmarks, including captioning, visual question answering, and visual dialogue. DeepMind never released Flamingo as a product or public API; it stayed a research model, but its architecture influenced later multimodal systems, including open reimplementations like OpenFlamingo and design choices in Google’s subsequent multimodal models.

item.title: Gato
item.description: Gato is a single neural network DeepMind introduced in May 2022 that the same set of weights can handle over 600 different tasks: playing Atari games, captioning images, holding a text conversation, and controlling a real robot arm to stack blocks. Instead of training separate models per task, DeepMind serialized every input, whether text, images, joint torques, or button presses, into one flat sequence of tokens and trained a single transformer on all of it at once, using an architecture similar to a large language model but with tokens standing in for actions and sensor data as well as words.

item.title: Gopher
item.description: Gopher is a 280-billion-parameter language model that DeepMind trained and described in a December 2021 paper as part of a study on how model performance scales with size. It was trained on MassiveText, a 10.5-terabyte corpus, and evaluated alongside five smaller models ranging from 44 million to 7 billion parameters to see how capability improved with scale. On the MMLU benchmark, Gopher scored 60% under a five-shot setup, a marked jump over prior models at the time.

item.title: Imagen
item.description: Imagen is Google Research’s original text-to-image diffusion model, described in a paper titled “Photorealistic Text-to-Image Diffusion Models with Deep Language Understanding” and posted to arXiv in May 2022. It pairs a large frozen language model, T5, with a cascade of diffusion models: a base model that generates a small 64x64 image, followed by two super-resolution stages that upsample it to 256x256 and then 1024x1024. The paper’s central finding was that scaling up the text encoder improved image quality and prompt alignment more than scaling up the image diffusion network itself, a result that influenced later text-to-image systems across the industry. Imagen reported a state-of-the-art FID score of 7.27 on the COCO benchmark despite never training on COCO data.

item.title: Med-PaLM
item.description: Med-PaLM is Google’s first attempt at a medical question-answering model, built by fine-tuning the 540B parameter PaLM model on clinical and consumer health data. Described in a paper posted in December 2022 and later published in Nature, it was the first AI system to score a passing grade on US Medical Licensing Examination style questions, clearing the roughly 60% bar. Google evaluated it on MultiMedQA, a benchmark it introduced alongside the model that pulls together medical exam questions, research literature queries, and the kinds of questions people search for about their own health.

item.title: Med-PaLM 2
item.description: Med-PaLM 2 is Google’s second-generation medical question-answering model, built on the PaLM 2 base and fine-tuned on medical domain data. It was the first language model to reach expert-level performance on the MedQA benchmark, a set of US Medical Licensing Examination style questions, scoring 86.5%, a jump of roughly 19 points over the original Med-PaLM. Google evaluated it across MultiMedQA, a collection of seven datasets spanning professional exams, medical research questions, and consumer health queries, and introduced a technique called ensemble refinement, where the model generates multiple reasoning paths and then combines them into a final answer.

item.title: Megatron-Turing NLG
item.description: Megatron-Turing NLG is a 530 billion parameter dense transformer language model that NVIDIA and Microsoft trained jointly and announced in October 2021. At the time it was the largest monolithic (non-mixture-of-experts) language model ever trained, built by combining NVIDIA’s Megatron-LM tensor-parallelism with Microsoft’s DeepSpeed pipeline-parallelism and ZeRO optimizer across hundreds of A100 GPUs. The model has 105 transformer layers and was trained on a 270 billion token corpus drawn from web text, books, and other curated sources.

item.title: Consensus
item.description: Consensus searches a large database of academic papers instead of the open web. You ask a question in plain language, such as whether a supplement improves sleep, and it returns an answer built from the studies it finds, with each claim linked to its source. For yes-or-no questions, the Consensus Meter shows how the papers split between yes, no, and mixed results. The result is a faster way to see what the evidence says without reading dozens of abstracts.

item.title: Dimensions
item.description:
Dimensions connects different kinds of research outputs. Instead of searching only for papers, users can see how a grant led to publications, which patents cite a study, and whether a trial or policy document refers to it. The linked structure helps trace the path from funding to impact.

Institutions, funders, and researchers use it for several purposes. Universities benchmark their output, funders track results of the grants they award, and companies look for experts and emerging fields. AI features summarize results, help with literature searches, and surface connections, and APIs let organizations pull data into their own systems.

item.title: Dovetail
item.description:
Dovetail gives research teams a home for customer feedback. Researchers upload interviews and other data, and the platform transcribes recordings, lets them highlight key quotes, and organizes everything so insights can be found later. Teams build a searchable repository instead of losing findings in slide decks.

AI shortens the analysis step. It tags content automatically, groups related feedback into themes, summarizes sessions, and answers questions across a body of research. Reports and shareable highlights help researchers communicate with product teams and executives, and integrations pull in data from support and survey tools.

item.title: Elicit
item.description:
Elicit helps researchers move through academic literature faster. A user asks a research question, and Elicit searches a large database of papers, presents relevant results, and extracts details such as sample size, methods, and outcomes into a table. Seeing structured comparisons across studies is much quicker than reading each paper in full.

Additional tools support systematic review work. Users can screen papers against criteria, summarize findings, and build reports, with citations tied to the passages in each paper so claims can be checked. It is used by students, academics, and professionals in evidence-based fields.

item.title: Elicit
item.description: Elicit is built for people who need to work through a large body of research. You ask a research question, and it finds relevant papers and shows a table with key details such as the study design, sample size, and results. You can add columns for the things you care about, and Elicit extracts the answers from each paper, so a review that might take days of reading can be started in an afternoon. Each extracted point links back to the passage in the paper it came from.

item.title: Explainpaper
item.description: Explainpaper targets a familiar frustration: academic papers are dense and full of jargon. You upload a PDF, select the sentence, equation, or paragraph you do not understand, and the tool gives a plain-language explanation. You can adjust the level, from a lay audience to an expert, and ask follow-up questions about the paper. It was popular with students and curious readers who wanted to follow a paper outside their own field.

item.title: Inciteful
item.description:
Inciteful takes a paper or a list of papers and builds a network of the research that surrounds them. Using citation data, it identifies the papers that are most connected, which tend to be foundational works, review articles, and recent developments. You enter a DOI, title, or several seed papers, and the tool shows a ranked list of papers, authors, and journals, with visual graphs of how they connect.

It is most useful early in a literature review. Starting from a few papers you know, you can discover similar and influential work you might have missed, track the most cited authors in the area, and spot new papers that cite your seeds. A Paper Discovery view finds the most important papers connected to your starting point, and a Literature Connector finds papers that link two different topics. Results can be exported to reference managers.

item.title: Lens.org
item.description:
The Lens aims to make innovation data open. It combines a very large database of patents from patent offices worldwide with scholarly works from sources like Crossref, PubMed, and others. Users can search by keywords, inventors, institutions, or classifications, and the results show patent families, legal status, citations, and links to the full text where available. The free access sets it apart from commercial patent databases.

The key feature is the connection between patents and papers. It tracks which scholarly works are cited in patents, which lets researchers and technology transfer offices see how academic research is used in inventions, and lets innovators find prior art. Collections let you save and share sets of results, and analytics and dashboards visualize trends, such as top applicants or fast-growing technology areas. Sequence search supports biotechnology patents.

item.title: NotebookLM Plus
item.description: NotebookLM Plus gives heavier users more room in NotebookLM, Google’s tool for working with your own documents. The free version lets you add sources, ask questions with citations, and generate study aids, but it limits the number of notebooks, sources, and daily queries. The Plus tier lifts those limits, so people with large projects, such as researchers, students writing theses, or analysts working across many documents, can keep more material in one place.

item.title: OpenRead
item.description:
OpenRead is built for people who read a lot of research. After you import a paper, an AI assistant can answer questions about it, explain terms, summarize sections, and pull out items like methods, results, and limitations. A structured summary view lays out the main points in a consistent format, which helps when scanning many papers for a review.

The platform extends beyond a single paper. It helps search the literature, organize papers into collections, take notes alongside the text, and generate outlines or review drafts from selected sources. Support for multiple languages makes it useful for researchers who read in a second language, and translation features help with papers published in other languages.

item.title: Paper Digest
item.description:
Paper Digest helps researchers keep up with a flood of new papers. Instead of scanning listings of new submissions every day, a user sets up topics or keywords and gets a personalized digest with short AI-generated summaries of matching papers. This helps researchers spot relevant work quickly and decide which papers merit a full read.

The service also publishes curated summaries of papers from major conferences and journals, and offers a platform to search, summarize, and organize papers. Paper Digest builds on text summarization models to produce abstracts and key points, and it provides tools such as a reader and a way to generate a quick literature overview. Some features are open to everyone, while others sit behind a login or subscription.

item.title: Perplexity
item.description: For research, Perplexity is useful because it shows its sources. Each answer comes with numbered citations to the pages it used, so you can open the link and check a claim before relying on it. You can narrow searches to particular kinds of sources, such as academic papers, and keep asking follow-up questions that build on the earlier ones. This makes it a quicker starting point than a list of search results for questions that need several sources.

item.title: Perplexity Labs
item.description: Labs goes beyond answering a question. You describe a project, such as a market analysis, a financial model, or a small dashboard, and Labs works for several minutes, combining web research, code execution, and chart creation. It then returns finished assets: a written report, a spreadsheet, charts, or a simple web app that you can download or share. The tool uses a team of specialized steps behind the scenes, so the output is more like a deliverable than a chat reply.

item.title: Perplexity Pages
item.description:
Pages is a publishing layer on top of Perplexity’s research. After you explore a topic with the assistant, you can convert the thread into a structured page with headings, summaries, and citations to the sources it used. It organizes the material in the way a short article or study guide would be written, instead of leaving you with a conversation log.

You control the result. Sections can be rewritten, reordered, or removed, images can be added, and the page can be published with a shareable link or kept private. Educators use Pages to create study guides, students for report drafts, and professionals for quick explainers on topics they research often. Because the citations travel with the content, readers can check where claims came from.

item.title: ResearchRabbit
item.description:
ResearchRabbit helps researchers find papers they would not discover through keyword search. You add a few papers to a collection, and the tool suggests related earlier work, later work that cites them, and papers by connected authors, showing the connections in visual graphs. As you add more papers, recommendations get more specific, which makes it behave like a recommendation engine for research.

Collections keep projects organized, and alerts notify you when new papers match your interests. You can see networks of authors, explore how a field evolved, and export references to managers like Zotero. It is popular with students and academics who are starting a literature review or entering a new topic, and who want something more exploratory than a search box.

item.title: Scholarcy
item.description:
Scholarcy tries to make reading faster. You give it an article or upload a PDF, and it breaks the document into a summary card with key points, the main findings, study design, limitations, and important terms. It extracts figures, tables, and references, and links the references so you can follow them. The format helps readers decide whether a paper is worth a full read.

A browser extension summarizes papers on publisher websites, and a library stores summaries with notes and tags. Export options send content to reference managers and note apps, and a feature can generate flashcards for study. Students and researchers use it to process large reading lists, create literature review notes, and check key details quickly.

item.title: Scinapse
item.description:
Scinapse is a search tool for scientific literature. It indexes a large body of scholarly papers across disciplines and ranks results with machine learning that considers relevance, citations, and recency. Users search by topic, title, or author, filter by year, journal, and field, and read abstracts with links to the publishers or open-access copies.

Features go beyond a basic list. Author pages show a researcher’s publications and citation profile, paper pages show who cited a work and related papers, and collections let you save papers to read later. Alerts notify you about new papers on a topic or from an author. The site was created by a Korean research technology company and is free to use, supported by its broader services for researchers.

item.title: SciSpace
item.description: SciSpace, formerly known as Typeset, is built around the problem of reading dense research. Upload a PDF or open a paper from its database, and an AI copilot lets you highlight a passage, a table, or an equation and ask for an explanation in simpler terms. You can also ask questions about the whole paper, request a summary, or get the key methods and results. It is helpful for students and researchers entering an unfamiliar field.

item.title: Semantic Scholar
item.description: Semantic Scholar is a research search engine built by the Allen Institute for AI, a nonprofit research organization. It covers hundreds of millions of academic papers across science, medicine, engineering, and the social sciences, and it is free. Unlike a plain keyword search, it uses language models to understand what papers are about and how they connect, which helps surface relevant work that does not use the exact words you typed.

item.title: Undermind
item.description: Undermind is designed for the situation where a simple search leaves you wondering what you missed. You describe your research question in plain language, including constraints and nuance, and the agent runs a deep search: it queries multiple sources, reads abstracts and text, follows citations, and refines its search based on what it finds. After some minutes, it delivers a ranked list of relevant papers with explanations of why each matches.

item.title: Wolfram Alpha AI
item.description: Wolfram Alpha doesn’t search the web. It computes answers. Ask it to integrate a function, convert units, compare populations, or show the weather on a given date, and it uses curated data and algorithms, written in the Wolfram Language, to produce a result with steps, charts, and data. That makes it reliable for math, physics, chemistry, statistics, and factual queries with definite answers, which is where language models often make mistakes.

item.title: Zotero
item.description:
Zotero saves references with a click. A browser connector captures a paper or web page along with its citation details and PDF, and the library organizes items in collections with tags and notes. Word and Google Docs plugins insert citations in thousands of styles.

Group libraries support collaboration, and the open ecosystem has plugins for annotation, syncing, and AI summaries and search. Because it is community driven and non-profit, users keep control over data.

item.title: Connected Papers
item.description: Connected Papers helps you get oriented in a research area. You enter a paper title, DOI, or link, and it produces a graph where each node is a paper and closer nodes are more similar. Similarity comes from co-citation and bibliographic coupling, meaning papers that cite similar sources or are cited together, rather than from keywords. Node size and color show citation count and year, which lets you see influential and recent work at a glance.

item.title: Iris.ai
item.description: Iris.ai aims to reduce the time scientists spend finding and reading relevant papers. Instead of keyword searches, a researcher can input a problem description or an abstract, and the system finds related papers by meaning. It then helps explore the results with a visual map of topics, filters based on content, and tools that extract data and summarize findings across many documents. Research teams use it to scan a field, check for prior work, and decide where to focus.

item.title: Litmaps
item.description: Litmaps helps researchers see a field instead of reading a list. You start with one or more papers you know, and the tool plots them on a map where one axis shows publication date and the other shows how much a paper is cited. Lines between the nodes show citation links. From the seeds, it suggests related papers that cite or are cited by your set, so you can quickly find missing foundational works and recent developments.

item.title: Scite
item.description: Scite changes how citation counts are read. A paper with many citations may be well supported or heavily disputed, and a raw count does not tell you which. Scite analyzes the text around each citation and labels it as supporting, contrasting, or mentioning, with a snippet of the citing sentence, so you can see how others have actually used a finding. It helps researchers judge reliability and spot controversial claims.
